facts.claim: The Fernandes–Lynch–Netemeyer meta-analysis covered 168 papers and 201 prior studies.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because pooling the literature allowed intervention effects to be compared across financial behaviors and delays.
facts.commonError: The 0.1-percent estimate came from one small classroom trial.
facts.whyWrong: It was a meta-analysis spanning a large research corpus.

facts.claim: The Bruns–Paunov review found 33 positive, 52 null, and two negative transparency effects across 87 tests.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because making a nudge visible generally left the mechanism intact and sometimes improved acceptance or attention.
facts.commonError: Every transparent nudge stopped working once participants noticed it.
facts.whyWrong: Only two tests reported a negative effect.

facts.claim: The publicity principle rejects a policy an architect could not acknowledge and defend publicly.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because public justification disciplines self-serving or covert uses of behavioral power.
facts.commonError: A policy is ethical whenever its behavior effect is statistically significant.
facts.whyWrong: Legitimacy and public reasons are separate from efficacy.

facts.claim: Paternalism of means helps people pursue their own ends rather than choosing those ends for them.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because the intervention targets attention, information, or self-control obstacles while preserving the chooser's underlying goal.
facts.commonError: Any welfare-oriented nudge imposes the architect's preferred way of life.
facts.whyWrong: Chooser-centered design uses the person's own considered interests as the standard.

facts.claim: Active choosing is itself a designed requirement and can be paternalistic.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because the architect forces a decision at a selected time even when the person would prefer delegation.
facts.commonError: Required choice is the neutral absence of influence.
facts.whyWrong: Forcing, timing, and framing the decision are all architectural choices.

facts.claim: Financial-education effects were negligible on behavior 20 months or more after intervention in the 2014 meta-analysis.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because knowledge and salience decay when instruction is separated from the decision context.
facts.commonError: One course permanently solves every later complex financial choice.
facts.whyWrong: Measured behavioral effects weakened with delay.

facts.claim: Boosts and nudges can be combined rather than treated as mutually exclusive.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because education builds competence while choice architecture supports action when time, attention, or complexity still constrain performance.
facts.commonError: Using a default prevents offering education.
facts.whyWrong: The tools operate on different barriers and can coexist.

facts.claim: Subliminal influence fails the transparency standard because the target cannot identify or contest it.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because a hidden stimulus bypasses the opportunity for reflective scrutiny and public accountability.
facts.commonError: Subliminal advertising is an ideal nudge whenever it preserves nominal options.
facts.whyWrong: Formal choice does not cure covert manipulation.

facts.claim: Mandates are warranted for conduct such as assault or theft because the chooser's freedom would impose direct harm on others.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because an easy opt-out would defeat the protective rule and leave victims exposed.
facts.commonError: A consistent nudge philosophy must oppose every ban and legal command.
facts.whyWrong: The presumption for choice is defeasible when serious third-party harm is at stake.
